issues.legal_issue: An award made on a private arbitration reference that affects qualifying rights in immovable property requires registration.
material_facts: An arbitrator appointed by the parties divided their joint immovable property into shares.
The award purported to effect a partition of immovable property valued above the applicable registration threshold.
issues.conclusion: The award required registration, and the appeal against the refusal to make it a rule of the court was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 17(1)(b) of the Registration Act, 1908 requires registration of a non-testamentary instrument that purports or operates to create, declare, assign, limit or extinguish rights in immovable property of the prescribed value. Whether the award’s rights can be enforced without further steps does not determine whether registration is required. The Court relied on M/s. Uttam Singh Dugal & Co. v. Union of India, Champalal v. Mst. Samarath Bai, and Kashinathsa Yamosa Kabadi v. Narsingsa Baskarsa Kabadi; it disapproved the contrary reasoning in Sheonarain Lal v. Prabhu Chand and Sardool Singh v. Hari Singh.

predicates.private_arbitration_reference: The parties refer their dispute to an arbitrator without the intervention of a court.
predicates.award_affects_immovable_property_rights: The arbitrator’s award purports or operates to affect rights in immovable property.
predicates.property_value_meets_registration_thresh: The affected immovable-property rights meet the applicable value threshold for compulsory registration.

issues.definition: When a private arbitration award affects immovable-property rights that meet the applicable value threshold, the award requires registration.

issues.legal_issue: An unregistered award affecting immovable property cannot be admitted in evidence to affect that property, although filing the award is not itself prohibited.
material_facts: The arbitrator applied to have the award filed and made a rule of the court.
An objection asserted that the unregistered award was inadmissible in evidence.
The award purported to effect a partition of immovable property.
issues.conclusion: Filing an unregistered award is not prohibited, but the award cannot be taken into evidence so as to affect immovable property for which registration is required.
issues.legal_principle: Section 49 of the Registration Act, 1908 does not prohibit filing an unregistered award; it prohibits using such an instrument as evidence to affect immovable property within section 17. The Court relied on Champalal v. Mst. Samarath Bai and Kashinathsa Yamosa Kabadi v. Narsingsa Baskarsa Kabadi.

rule.if: award_filing_proceeding and award_offered_to_affect_immovable_property and registration_required and award_unregistered

predicates.award_filing_proceeding: A party seeks to have an arbitration award filed in court or made a rule of the court.
predicates.award_offered_to_affect_immovable_proper: The award is offered as evidence to affect rights in immovable property.
predicates.registration_required: The award affects immovable-property rights that require registration.
predicates.award_unregistered: The award has not been registered.

issues.definition: In a court proceeding to file an award, an unregistered award that is offered to affect property requiring registration cannot be used as evidence for that purpose.

issues.legal_issue: An arbitration award may have binding legal effect and create rights before it is made a decree, even though enforcement of those rights requires further steps.
material_facts: The parties referred claims concerning joint property to an arbitrator.
The arbitrator issued an award dividing the property between the parties.
The dispute concerned whether the award had legal effect before a court made it a decree.
issues.conclusion: The award was not a mere waste paper: it had legal effect, and the rights it created could not be enforced until it was made a decree of the court.
issues.legal_principle: Paragraph 7 of the First Schedule to the Arbitration Act, 1940 provides that an award is final and binding on the parties and persons claiming under them. Claims referred to arbitration merge in the award, and the original claims cannot thereafter be pursued as such. The Court relied on M/s. Uttam Singh Dugal & Co. v. Union of India and the reasoning in Bhajahari Saha Banikya v. Behary Lal Basak; it also distinguished the creation of a right from its enforceability before a decree is made.

predicates.private_arbitration_award: The parties obtain an award through arbitration without the intervention of a court.
predicates.award_determines_referred_claims: The award decides claims that the parties submitted to arbitration.
predicates.award_purports_to_create_property_rights: The award purports to create or determine rights in property.

issues.definition: When a private arbitration award determines referred claims and purports to create property rights, it creates rights before a decree, but those rights require a decree for enforcement.
